catalog_quote: Surprisingly, there are no previously published studies of Iñupiaq prosody, including stress or lack thereof. ... Furthermore, Kaplan (1994b) cites S. Jacobson (undated), saying Iñupiaq has no prosody at all, a dubious and typologically unlikely claim. Listening to Iñupiaq, there is an intuitive sense that at least one syllable per word is more prominent than any others; whether this syllable prominence is lexical stress or not remains to be seen, as there is no a priori reason to assume that lexical stress is a salient feature of Iñupiaq. Furthermore, it may be prosodically motivated or morphologically motivated prominence (cf. Tuttle (2000:35–36) for Apache). I will use SYLLABLE PROMINENCE and STRESS interchangeably here and leave the status of stress as a possible meaning-bearing unit in Iñupiaq for later study. new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand treatment states that Malimiut (North Alaskan) Iñupiaq words have one perceptually prominent syllable, but the author explicitly leaves open whether this is lexical stress and gives no rule for its location; acoustically the prominence is cued by F0, intensity, loudness and spectral tilt, not duration; there is no Yupik-style rhythmic (alternating) stress or iambic lengthening. Kaplan (2001, quoted ibid.) says rhythmic stress systems are absent from Inuit; Kaplan 1981's NAI phonology has no stress section and equates English stress with Iñupiaq vowel length in loans.
new_statements.exceptions: None; author notes Kaplan (1994b, after Jacobson) claimed Iñupiaq 'has no prosody at all', which she rejects as typologically unlikely.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level perceptual 'syllable prominence' in elicited Malimiut Coastal (Kotzebue area) speech, based on the author's unpublished 2008 acoustic study; placement (word vs phrase, citation forms) not analysed.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Lanz 2010) describes the Malimiut Coastal dialect (Kotzebue Sound Inupiatun, Glottolog kotz1238, under Malimiutun mali1289, a dialect of nort2943). The other NAI descriptions examined (Kaplan 1979/1981, MacLean 1993/2012, Nagai 2006) cover Barrow/North Slope (nort2944) and Kobuk (kobu1239) and are silent on stress. Kaplan 1985's explicit stress rule (non-final closed syllables and long vowels stressed) is for King Island / Seward Peninsula Inupiaq, a different Glottolog language (nort2945, Bering Strait dialect king1259), not nort2943.

sources.note: Sec. 2.7 'Stress' (pp.42-46): no prior published study of Inupiaq prosody; perceptually at least one syllable per word is more prominent but whether this is lexical stress is undetermined; placement rules not established; her phonetic study (Lanz 2008) found F0, intensity, loudness, spectral tilt significant cues, duration not; no Yupik-type rhythmic lengthening; cites Kaplan (2001) that rhythmic stress systems are absent from Inuit and Kaplan (1994b, citing Jacobson) that Inupiaq 'has no prosody at all' (which she calls dubious).

sources.note: Krauss intro p.1: Inuit has a simple long/short vowel and consonant contrast 'largely unaffected by whatever stress, pitch or other features that may be superimposed in higher-level prosody' (general Inuit). Kaplan p.193: for King Island (Seward Peninsula, nort2945) 'the non-final closed syllables and all long vowels... receive stress'; NAI is said to lack consonant gradation but no NAI stress rule is given.
